title: Exercise Tier Lists are STUPID
summary: NH argues that exercise tier lists, including his own, just pass on the maker's subjective values, but says rejecting all hierarchies is a dangerous relativism. He then gives and ranks the 10 metrics he uses to judge a lift for hypertrophy: enjoyment first, then progression consistency, active range of motion, ease of use, stimulus-to-fatigue ratio, stability, joints, cardio impact, comfort and soreness. He ends by calling for critical thinking about the hidden value systems of fitness influencers.
claims: Tier lists are the easiest format for views and engagement because they trigger emotion (people defend favourite lifts in the comments) and fear of missing out on a magic lift
He put the incline curl in C tier, got furious reactions, and later realised it was S tier: he had just been bad at it, not the lift
Every tier list downloads its maker's subjectivity: creators like or dislike a lift first and then find reasons, which is why tier lists from different YouTubers never match
Concluding that all lifts are equal is a dangerous relativism; hierarchies are useful when they are built on objective principles and metrics

Stability means how easily you hold the body and joints at the right angle to hit the target muscle; a seated dumbbell press beats a standing overhead press because hips, knees and torso lean are removed

Stimulus-to-fatigue must be judged per target muscle: hamstring curls beat deadlifts on SFR for hamstrings, though deadlifts give more total stimulus; preacher curls beat barbell cheat curls for biceps
He considers the pullover a lats or triceps lift, not a chest lift; its resistance profile is debated
Low cardiovascular impact matters because a lift should let you reach muscular failure before cardiovascular failure
He carries the Husafell stone hugged like a big pot with hands underneath because the normal grip wrecks his biceps and forearm tendons; it is harder but more comfortable
Soreness ranks last (10th): it is inconsistent between people, fades as the muscle adapts, and can just signal poor recovery capacity
Yet a lift that keeps making you sore for years gives a really good workout; RDLs always leave his hamstrings and glutes very sore, so he keeps them
Soreness is a practical tool to find which muscle a lift hits, e.g. some people get sore triceps from pullovers

Comfort ranks 9th: bodybuilders seek comfort, unlike strongmen, because a stable comfortable setup lets you push deep into the discomfort of real failure; preacher curls over your knees will never reach true failure
Pain distracts from being in the muscle; that's why everyone pads the bar for hip thrusts
Getting winded by curls or squats means poor conditioning, not a bad lift; cardio makes you a better bodybuilder
Bodybuilders should do 10-15 minutes of high-intensity cardio plus low-intensity work like hikes and swimming, and supersets add conditioning without hurting performance
Split squats with an SSB or Smith machine are better for bodybuilders than holding dumbbells: you get stronger with less cardiovascular strain
Joint friendliness ranks 7th for him but climbs with training age; a lifter in his 40s might rank it 2nd or 3rd because tendons, not muscles, become the limit
Starting bodybuilding at 30-40 is hard not because you can't build muscle but because joints are beaten up, especially for ex-strength or college athletes
Natural bodybuilding strengthens tendons, but only so far: triceps are limited by elbow tendon health, quads by the knees
Bodybuilders are not movement enthusiasts; it's fine to drop lifts that feel bad instead of forcing adaptation

Wrist curls with a fixed dumbbell feel horrible on the wrist and miss the forearm; flat barbell bench that hurts shoulders can be swapped for dumbbells; use an EZ bar if a straight bar gives biceps tendinitis
Stability ranks 6th: bodybuilders choose boring, stable lifts over flashy ones because the goal is to look impressive, not to lift impressively
The Smith machine was created by Jack LaLanne to get heavy loading with stability, and every serious bodybuilding gym has one
Cables are for people who train hard: cuffed cable lateral raises allow more weight and reps than dumbbells because the line of pull stays fixed and the stack controls the negative
Stimulus-to-fatigue ranks only 5th for him: it is often used as an excuse to avoid heavy free-weight compounds, and fatigue is part of stimulus
SFR matters most for small muscles: once you isolate forearms, biceps, triceps, calves, core, traps and more, fatigue piles up and drops frequency, set quality and effective volume
Intensity is super important for hypertrophy and may be the name of the game
Israetel's big-mover approach ignores SFR while Nippard's complex days need low-fatigue lifts; each creator's view follows his own methodology
Ease of use ranks 4th: a lift taking more than 3 minutes to set up will end up skipped
He dropped a cable upper-chest press that only felt right 20% of the time for dumbbell incline press, which gives about 90% of the result
Active range of motion / mechanical tension ranks 3rd; everyone agrees it matters but no one agrees which lift loads what or where
Science-based fitness creators bicker more than anyone, like old ladies at the park
Progression consistency ranks 2nd: if you can't progressively overload a lift, nothing else about it matters
After the novice stage, biceps isolations progressing 5-10 lb a year is normal and not a sign of a bad lift
If a lift doesn't progress for you, ditch it for another variation of the same pattern; his bench plateaued for years while weighted dips progressed steadily
Enjoyment ranks 1st and trumps every objective metric: a lift you don't enjoy gets skipped and done without intensity, so it gives no progress
Someone enjoying a random program will beat someone hating a perfect one, because consistency drives results in everything
Other influencers leave enjoyment off their lists entirely, and many pros would rank soreness much higher
How a muscle looks while you train it is a useless metric, yet much Instagram content promotes lifts for exactly that; strength athletes push lifts for looking badass
Influencers often push lifts they just started enjoying, or bash ones they personally suck at, so tier lists go obsolete within a year
Critical thinking means judging an opinion by the value system that produced it; most fitness influencers aren't even aware of their own
He invites other natural creators to publish their own top-10 hypertrophy metrics, and viewers to post theirs
